Finite Automata State Graphs 
67
•
They are widely used in compiler design, lexical analysis, pattern matching, communication 
protocols, and digital system design.

A Simple Example 
• A finite automaton that accepts only “1”.
68
• Another Simple Example
• A finite automaton accepting Zero or any number of 1’s followed by a single 0
• Alphabet: {0,1}

And Another Example 
• Alphabet {0,1}
• What language does this recognize?
69
•
It remains in the initial state while reading 1’s.
•
the automaton accepts all binary strings whose last two or more symbols are consecutive zeros 
(ending with "00").

And Another Example 
• Alphabet still { 0, 1 } 
• The operation of the automaton is not completely defined by the input
 
– On input “11” the automaton could be in either state 
• Unlike deterministic automata, the next state is not uniquely determined by the current state and 
input symbol. 
• Such machines are called Non-Deterministic Finite Automata (NFAs).
70

Epsilon Moves 
• Another kind of transition: ε-moves (allows an automaton to move from one state to another 
without consuming any input symbol.)
• Machine can move from state A to state B without reading input .
• During implementation, ε-transitions are eventually eliminated while converting the NFA into an 
equivalent DFA. 
71

Deterministic and Non-Deterministic Automata 
72
• Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA)
– One transition per input per state
– No ε-moves
• Non-deterministic Finite Automata (NFA)
– Can have multiple transitions for one input in a given state
– Can have ε-moves
• Finite automata have finite memory
 
– meaning they store only the current state and cannot remember an arbitrary amount of 
 
past input.

Execution of Finite Automata 
• A DFA can take only one path through the state graph
• Completely determined by input
• The sequence of states is completely determined by the input, making DFA execution 
straightforward and efficient.
• NFAs can choose
• Whether to make ε-moves
• Which of multiple transitions for a single input to take 
73

• NFA can be in multiple states simultaneously after reading an input symbol.
• The acceptance rule for an NFA is simple: if at least one possible path ends in a final (accepting) state 
after processing the complete input, the string is accepted. 
• Otherwise, the input string is rejected.
74
Acceptance of NFAs

NFA vs. DFA (1)
• NFAs and DFAs recognize the same set of languages (regular languages)
• DFAs are easier to implement
 
– There are no choices to consider 
• For a given language the NFA can be simpler than the DFA 
• DFA can be exponentially larger than NFA 
75

Regular Expressions to Finite Automata 
• High-level sketch 
76

Regular Expressions to NFA (1) 
• To automatically generate lexical analyzers, every regular expression is first converted into an 
equivalent Non-Deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA).
 
– Notation: NFA for regular expression M 
77

Regular Expressions to NFA (2) 
78

Thompson's construction combines smaller NFAs to build 
automata for more complex regular expressions.
These recursive construction rules ensure that every regular expression 
can be systematically transformed into an equivalent NFA.

Example of Regular Expression → NFA conversion 
• Consider the regular expression: (1+0)*1 
• The NFA is

•

•
automaton is concatenated with another NFA for 1.

NFA to DFA. The Trick   
• Although NFAs are simple to construct, DFAs are easier to execute efficiently. 
• Therefore, every NFA is converted into an equivalent DFA using the subset construction algorithm. 
• In this method, each DFA state represents a subset of NFA states rather than a single state. 
• The DFA start state is the ε-closure of the NFA start state, containing all states reachable through ε-
transitions. 
• For each input symbol, transitions are computed by finding all reachable NFA states and then taking 
their ε-closure. 
• This process continues until no new subsets are generated. 
• The resulting DFA recognizes exactly the same language as the original NFA.
80

Subset Construction Algorithm
• Start from the NFA start state and compute its ε-closure. 
• Treat this ε-closure as the first DFA state. 
• For each DFA state and each input symbol, compute the reachable states and 
their ε-closure. 
• Add the resulting subset as a new DFA state if it has not been seen before. 
• Record the transition in the DFA transition table. 
• Repeat until no new subsets are created. 
• Mark any subset containing an NFA final state as a DFA final state
81

NFA to DFA. Remark 
• During execution, an NFA can be in multiple states simultaneously because of multiple transitions 
and ε-moves. 
• To simulate this behavior using a DFA, each DFA state represents a subset of NFA states. 
• If an NFA has N states, it may occupy any subset of these states at a given time. 
• The total number of possible subsets is 2ᴺ (including the empty set), or 2ᴺ − 1 non-empty subsets. 
• Therefore, an equivalent DFA may require up to 2ᴺ states in the worst case. 
• This explains why DFA construction can lead to an exponential increase in the number of states.
82

NFA to DFA Example 
83
•
Start with the NFA
•
Find the ε-closure of the start state A,  ε-closure (A) = 
{A, B, C, D, H, I}, it will be the start state of the DFA
•
Each DFA state represents a set of NFA states.
•
Compute transitions
•
From ABCDHI: 
•
On input 0, the NFA reaches F, then ε-
transitions add G, A, B, C, D, H, I. 
•
New DFA state: FGABCDHI
•
On input 1, the NFA reaches E, then ε-
transitions add J, G, A, B, C, D, H, I. 
•
New DFA state: EJGABCDHI
•
Any DFA state containing the NFA final state J becomes 
an accepting state.

DFA Implementation Using a Transition Table
• A DFA can be implemented by a 2D table T
 
– One dimension is “states”
 
– Other dimension is “input symbols”
 
– For every transition Si →a Sk define T[i,a] = k
• DFA “execution”
 
– If in state Si and input a, read T[i,a] = k and skip to state Sk
 
- Very efficient 
84

Table Implementation of a DFA 
85
•
NFA → DFA conversion is at the heart of tools such as lex, ML-Lex or flex
•
But, DFAs can be huge (large number of states after NFA-to-DFA conversion)
•
Practical lexer generators balance speed and memory usage by selecting efficient automata 
representations and optimization techniques.

Theory vs Practice 
• Two differences:
• DFAs recognize lexemes. A lexer must return a type of acceptance (token type) 
rather than simply an accept/reject indication.
• DFAs consume the complete string and accept or reject it. A lexer must find the 
end of the lexeme in the input stream and then find the next one, etc.
